newsitem.title: USA: Reporter apologizes to Peru hostage families.
newsitem.headline: Reporter apologizes to Peru hostage families.

text.p: A Japanese TV reporter who sneaked into the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence last week, apologised on Sunday to the families of the hostages for his action.

Tsuyoshi Hitomi, a jouranlist with a subsidiary of TV Asahi who gave a news conference after arriving from Peru early on Sunday, said he was "surprised" that police had detained him but felt he had not put the hostages' lives in danger by his actions.

"I do apologise for causing worry to the families of the hostages and the International Red Cross workers and others," said the 26-year-old Hitomi, who had not told his superiors he was going into the residence.
He was released on Saturday by anti-terrorist police in Lima after being detained for four days.
Hitomi said he did not feel he was jeopardising the negotiating efforts because there had not been any reported progress on the hostage situation for several days.

The Peruvian and Japanese governments were infuriated by Hitoshi and his Peruvian interpreter, Victor Borja, saying they, and a previous impromptu press conference in the residence, set back negotiations and prevented the release of more hostages by denying the government an important bargaining chip of deciding when to grant the MRTA publicity.

Speaking through an interpreter, Hitomi, who is based in New York, said a two-hour video taped meeting he had with Nestor Cerpa, the Tupac Amaru Revoluntionary Movement (MRTA) guerrilla leader and a Japanese hostage called Kobayashi, was confiscated and given to the Japanese Foreign Ministry.
He said he and Borja had gone through the gate of a private residence where they were staked out, onto the road outside the residence and simply walked up to the front door.
"Without any police restrictions, we were able to go the front door of the residence. We got to the front door easily and quickly decided to go in and gather information," Hitomi said.
He said after showing a guerrilla identification, he was given access to Cerpa and the Japanese hostage, a businessman with Mitsui Bussan in Peru.
Hitomi said he left after his camera battery died.
